text: Oliver Heaviside (/ˈhɛvisaɪd/ HEV-ee-syde; 18 May 1850 – 3 February 1925) was a British mathematician and electrical engineer who invented a new technique for solving differential equations, equivalent to the Laplace transform, independently developed vector calculus, and rewrote Maxwell's equations in the form commonly used today. He significantly shaped the understanding and application of Maxwell's equations in the decades following Maxwell's death. In 1893, he extended them to gravitoelectromagnetism, which was confirmed by Gravity Probe B in 2005. His formulation of the telegrapher's equations became commercially important during his lifetime, after their significance was initially overlooked, as few others were familiar with his novel methodology. Born on 18 May 1850 at 55 Kings Street (now Plender Street) in Camden Town, England, the youngest of three children of Thomas Heaviside, a draughtsman and wood engraver, and Rachel Elizabeth West, Heaviside was a short and red-headed child who suffered from scarlet fever, resulting in a hearing impairment that hindered his communication and social interactions as a child. He described his time in Kings Street as miserable, which led him to hate craftspeople and influenced his lifelong abstention from alcohol. A small legacy allowed the family to move to a better part of Camden when he was thirteen, and he was sent to Camden House Grammar School, where he placed fifth out of five hundred pupils in 1865. His parents could not keep him at school after he turned 16, so he studied independently for a year with no further formal education. His uncle by marriage, Sir Charles Wheatstone (1802–1875), an expert in telegraphy and electromagnetism, took a strong interest in his education, and in 1867 sent him to work with his older brother Arthur Wheatstone in Newcastle-upon-Tyne. Two years later, he took a job as a telegraph operator with the Danish Great Northern Telegraph Company laying a cable from Newcastle to Denmark using British contractors, where he soon became an electrician. He continued studying while working, and by age 22 published an article in the Philosophical Magazine on 'The Best Arrangement of Wheatstone's Bridge for measuring a Given Resistance with a Given Galvanometer and Battery,' which received positive feedback from physicists including Sir William Thomson and James Clerk Maxwell. When he published an article on the duplex method of using a telegraph cable, he mocked R. S. Culley, the engineer in chief of the Post Office telegraph system, who had dismissed duplex as impractical. In 1873, his application to join the Society of Telegraph Engineers was rejected with the comment "they didn't want telegraph clerks," which angered Heaviside, prompting him to ask Thomson to sponsor him, and with the support of the society's president, he was admitted "despite the P.O. snobs." In 1873, Heaviside encountered Maxwell's Treatise on Electricity and Magnetism, which he later recalled as "great, greater and greatest," and despite his initial ignorance of mathematical analysis, he spent several years mastering it before moving to his own interpretation of Maxwell's work. From home, he developed transmission line theory (the "telegrapher's equations"), showing mathematically that uniformly distributed inductance in a telegraph line would reduce both attenuation and distortion, and that with sufficient inductance and low insulation resistance, the circuit would be distortionless, allowing all frequencies to propagate at equal speeds. From 1882 to 1902, except for three years, Heaviside contributed regular articles to the trade paper The Electrician, which paid him £40 per year—insufficient for living but aligned with his desire to write. Between 1883 and 1887, he averaged 2–3 articles per month, which later formed the bulk of his Electromagnetic Theory and Electrical Papers. In 1880, he researched the skin effect and patented in England the coaxial cable. In 1884, he recast Maxwell's mathematical analysis from its original form (using quaternions) into modern vector terminology, reducing twelve of the original twenty equations in twenty unknowns to four differential equations in two unknowns—now known as Maxwell's equations—describing electric charges (static and moving), magnetic fields, and their relationship. Between 1880 and 1887, he developed the operational calculus using the differential operator p (previously denoted by D by Boole), providing a method of solving differential equations by treating them as algebraic equations. This caused controversy due to its lack of rigor; Heaviside famously stated, "Mathematics is an experimental science, and definitions do not come first, but later on. They make themselves, when the nature of the subject has developed itself," and once asked, "Shall I refuse my dinner because I do not fully understand the process of digestion?" In 1887, Heaviside worked with his brother Arthur on a paper titled "The Bridge System of Telephony," proposing the addition of loading coils (inductors) to telephone and telegraph lines to correct distortion. The paper was blocked by William Henry Preece of the Post Office, who viewed self-inductance as detrimental to transmission and had recently dismissed the editor of The Electrician, which ended Heaviside's long-running series of articles until 1891. Heaviside believed Preece was behind the sacking and considered him mathematically incompetent, a view supported by biographer Paul J. Nahin, who described Preece as "a powerful government official, enormously ambitious, and in some remarkable ways, an utter blockhead." Preece suppressed Heaviside's work to protect his own reputation and avoid admitting error. The importance of Heaviside's work remained unrecognized for some time. In 1897, AT&T employed George A. Campbell and Michael I. Pupin to extend Heaviside's work, filing patents for their research and the construction of coils previously invented by Heaviside. AT&T later offered Heaviside money in exchange for his rights, possibly influenced by their respect for his work, but Heaviside refused unless the company granted him full recognition. He was chronically poor, making his refusal especially notable. In 1959, Norbert Wiener published The Tempter and accused AT&T and Michael I. Pupin of usurping Heaviside's inventions. This setback redirected Heaviside's attention to electromagnetic radiation; in 1888 and 1889, he calculated field deformations around a moving charge, predicting what is now known as Cherenkov radiation and inspiring George FitzGerald to propose the Lorentz–FitzGerald contraction. In 1889, he first published a correct derivation of the magnetic force on a moving charged particle, the magnetic component of the Lorentz force. In the late 1880s and early 1890s, Heaviside worked on electromagnetic mass, treating it as material mass capable of producing similar effects; Wilhelm Wien later verified his expression for low velocities. In 1891, the British Royal Society named him a Fellow, and the following year devoted over fifty pages of the Philosophical Transactions to his vector methods and electromagnetic theory. He was elected to honorary membership of the Manchester Literary and Philosophical Society in 1894. In 1905, he received an honorary doctorate from the University of Göttingen. In 1896, FitzGerald and John Perry granted Heaviside a civil list pension of £120 per year, which he accepted after rejecting other charitable offers from the Royal Society. In 1902, Heaviside proposed the existence of the Kennelly–Heaviside layer of the ionosphere, suggesting a mechanism for radio signals to travel around the Earth's curvature. The layer's existence was confirmed in 1923. His predictions, combined with Planck's radiation theory, likely discouraged further attempts to detect solar radio waves until Jansky's development of radio astronomy in 1932. Heaviside opposed Albert Einstein's theory of relativity; Howard Eves noted he was the only first-rate physicist at the time to criticize Einstein, with his invectives often bordering on absurdity. In later years, Heaviside became eccentric; according to B.A. Behrend, he became a recluse who delivered manuscripts to a grocery store where editors picked them up. Though he had been an active cyclist in his youth, his health declined in his sixth decade. During this time, he signed letters with the initials "W.O.R.M." and reportedly painted his fingernails pink, moving granite blocks into his house as furniture. In 1922, he became the first recipient of the Faraday Medal, established that year. He was a Unitarian but not religious, and reportedly mocked people who placed faith in a supreme being. He died on 3 February 1925 in Torquay at age 74 after falling from a ladder. He is buried just behind and to the right of the building near the southeast corner of Paignton cemetery, with his father Thomas and mother Rachel. The gravestone was cleaned by an anonymous donor in 2005. He was highly regarded by electrical engineers, especially after his correction to Kelvin's transmission line analysis was vindicated, though most recognition came posthumously. In July 2014, academics at Newcastle University and the Newcastle Electromagnetics Interest Group founded the Heaviside Memorial Project to restore the monument through public subscription. The restored memorial was unveiled on 30 August 2014 by Alan Heather, a distant relative of Heaviside, and attended by the Mayor of Torbay, the MP for Torbay, an ex-curator of the Science Museum (representing the Institution of Engineering and Technology), the Chairman of the Torbay Civic Society, and delegates from Newcastle University. A collection of Heaviside's papers is held at the Institution of Engineering and Technology (IET) Archive Centre, including notebooks with mathematical equations, annotated pamphlets on telegraphy, manuscript notes, drafts of papers, correspondence, and drafts of articles for 'Electromagnetic Theory.' An audio tribute from 1950 by Oliver E. Buckley, President of Bell Telephone Labs, has been digitized and is accessible on the IET Archives. In 1908, Heaviside was made an Honorary Member of the Institution of Electrical Engineers (IEE), with his entry reading "1908 Oliver Heaviside FRS" in the IEE Roll of Honorary Members and Faraday Medallists 1871–1921. In 1922, he received the Faraday Medal. In 1950, the IEE Council established the Heaviside Premium Award, recommending a £10 annual prize for the best mathematical paper accepted. Heaviside advanced vector methods and vector calculus; Maxwell's original formulation consisted of 20 equations in 20 variables, which Heaviside reduced to four equations in four variables (B, E, J, and ρ) using curl and divergence operators. Less well known is that Heaviside's equations and Maxwell's are not identical, and it is easier to modify Heaviside's version to align with quantum physics. He also discussed the possibility of gravitational waves using the analogy between the inverse-square law in gravitation and electricity. With quaternion multiplication, the square of a vector is negative, which displeased Heaviside; he is credited by C. J. Joly with developing hyperbolic quaternions, though this was largely the work of Alexander Macfarlane. He invented the Heaviside step function to calculate current when a circuit is switched on and was the first to use the unit impulse function now known as the Dirac delta function. He developed his operational calculus method for solving linear differential equations, which resembles the current Laplace transform method based on the "Bromwich integral," named after Bromwich who provided a rigorous justification for Heaviside's operator method using contour integration. Heaviside was familiar with the Laplace transform but considered his method more direct. He developed transmission line theory (the "telegrapher's equations"), which increased transmission rates over transatlantic cables by a factor of ten—reducing transmission time from ten minutes per character to one minute per character—and discovered that telephone transmission could be improved by adding electrical inductance in series with the cable. He also independently discovered the Poynting vector. He advanced the idea that the Earth's upper atmosphere contained an ionized layer, predicting the Kennelly–Heaviside layer. In 1947, Edward Appleton received the Nobel Prize in Physics for proving the layer's existence. He coined several terms in electromagnetic theory; however, he is sometimes incorrectly credited with coining susceptance (the imaginary part of admittance), which was coined by Charles Proteus Steinmetz in 1894, and reactance (the imaginary part of impedance), which was coined by Édouard Hospitalier in 1893.

Placing electrical inductance in series with the cable could significantly improve performance, and Heaviside independently discovered the Poynting vector. He proposed that the Earth's uppermost atmosphere contains an ionised layer, later known as the ionosphere, which he predicted was the Kennelly–Heaviside layer; this layer was later confirmed by Edward Appleton, who received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1947 for proving its existence. Heaviside introduced several key terms in electromagnetic theory. However, he is sometimes mistakenly credited with coining susceptance (the imaginary part of admittance) and reactance (the imaginary part of impedance); in fact, susceptance was introduced by Charles Proteus Steinmetz in 1894, and reactance was introduced by Édouard Hospitalier in 1893.
